title: Caveman leadership and the CDO*
content:
We don’t have written records, but I’m imagining that groups of cavemen made decisions around the fire in largely the same way we run sophisticated organizations today.

About a hundred years ago, three disciplines helped create the modern world:

Scientific management used a stopwatch and the assembly line to relentlessly improve the productivity of the industrial age.

Scientific advertising brought measurement and rigor to the work of creating ads and buying media.

And engineering brought physics and the scientific method to everything we build. Bridges don’t fall down, computer chips get faster and cheaper and the things we make rarely break.

But the bosses still do what they always did. They place comfort and convenience over effectiveness. If the hard-working people in any other part of the organization approached their work the way they do, it wouldn’t last.

One estimate is that the direct labor cost of time spent in meetings at a Fortune 500 company is over a quarter of a _billion_ dollars a year. Per company.

And yet, meetings occur regularly, with no measurable outputs. Few people do the reading or prep, and many show up late or uninformed. The room isn’t designed for the purpose it’s being used for, and no one is taking notes or sending out follow-up action requests.

There’s rarely an interlocutor–a neutral moderator who asks questions, guides the conversation and leads the group to a decision. People are rarely given feedback on their meeting productivity, and aren’t encouraged to get training or improve their skills.

You’ve probably been to a thousand meetings. How many can you remember that achieved what could have happened with that much time and talent invested?

In my experience at large organizations, the physical dynamic in the room is often left to the facilities person who ran the AV cart in high school or the office supply vendor who was asked to fill a square room with furniture that would serve many purposes. That’s not how we invest in an assembly line or a semiconductor fab…

And many decisions, if implemented, remain unexamined. There’s little time or focus invested in learning from what came before, and no one is keeping track of whether the loud voices are usually right. Famous CEOs shoot from the hip, and seem to think that wrong action fast is better than thoughtfully doing the right thing tomorrow.

Corporate culture usually pushes people to avoid speaking up, to prize comfort over progress, and to support the status quo unless there’s an emergency. We either invite too many or not enough people into group decisions, and end up using superficial or extraneous information to make choices.

We reject a job applicant because they had parsley in their teeth, didn’t go to a famous college or they don’t look like us. Deniability often seems more important than progress. We use easy proxies and measures instead of the ones that really matter. And we repeat patterns that worked with the old systems, but make no sense with the new ones.

*The job of the Chief Decision Officer, then, isn’t to make decisions. It’s to create the conditions for the organization to do a better job of it. Not only at a Fortune 500 company, but at a thriving non-profit, a government agency or a small start-up.

Surgeons scrub before entering the OR. It’s hygienic, but also a ritual. It reminds them that this place is special, it has a purpose, rules and outcomes. Don’t come in if you’re not prepared to do your part.

The CDO ought to establish the same approach for the way we make decisions and take action on those decisions.

# Mother Bats’ Hearts Quicken When They Hear Baby’s Cries

Like humans, bat moms are primed by evolution to spring into action

[DR](http://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

By [Devin Reese](http://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

6:30 PM CDT on October 23, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/AdobeStock_43134376.jpeg?w=2880)

Sweet baby bat on my finger.

The cries of babies are not just a nuisance. They are calls for help, honed by evolution to spur an immediate, ingrained response. When a human mother hears her baby crying, [her brain elicits a “do-or-die” response](https://www.maynoothuniversity.ie/faculty-science-engineering/news/adults-brains-rapidly-respond-cries-baby-says-study) in neuronal activity in the midbrain’s survival region.

A [new study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ethology/articles/10.3389/fetho.2026.1891633/full) published this week in _Frontiers in Ethology_ reported that it’s not just human mothers that react physiologically to their baby’s cries; some bat mothers do too.

**Read more: “**[**The Social Life of Bats**](https://nautil.us/the-social-life-of-bats-373018)**”**

Neuroethologists from Japan studied the responses of captive Japanese house bats (_Pipistrellus abramus_) to their pup’s “isolation” calls—squeaky clicks that warn the mother that it’s lost or needs help.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

“The inspiration for our study began with a striking observation in our laboratory colony,” said lead study author Kazuki Yoshino-Hashizawa from Doshisha University. “When a pup was separated from their roosting area, only the biological mother immediately rushed over to bring it back.”

The study started with four pregnant bats, which each gave birth to a litter of three pups. When the pups were just two days old, the researchers used ultrasonic microphones to record their isolation calls. At 30 days old, when they’d become independent and transitioned to the echolocation calls used for hunting, those were recorded too. The two types of calls were then played back to the mothers shortly after the pups had matured.

The results showed that a bat mother reacted exclusively to the recorded isolation calls of her own pups. Based on ECG recordings, her heart rate increased by as much as 70 beats per minute, showing that she was physiologically stirred by the baby’s unique sound. Her responsiveness undoubtedly helps a Japanese house bat find her own offspring among the hundreds of bats in a colony by priming her body for action.

Surprisingly, a mother’s physiological response to the echolocation calls of her mature offspring was even stronger, perhaps because she’d gotten to know the pup’s sounds better. The calls of bat pups change daily as they mature, leading the study authors to hypothesize that “mothers’ recognition abilities may undergo continuous adaptation,” as they wrote in the paper.

Unexpectedly, the study authors also detected a heart rate response of mothers to calls of unfamiliar adult males. While this shows additional complexity in bat social behavior, it was impossible to determine whether it was a positive arousal reaction or a negative reaction to a perceived threat.

Regardless, mother bats’ hearts are beating to the sounds of their colony. ![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Ice Age Europeans Were More Connected Than We Thought
content:
Europe is a continent that’s rich in history, but it’s also rich in prehistory. Sifting through the remains of tools, dwellings, and other artifacts, archaeologists have discovered a succession of distinct cultures. The Gravettian culture, which existed from roughly 33,000 to 22,000 years ago, were hunter-gatherers known for crafting tanged arrowheads and carving Venus figurines from mammoth ivory.

Although the Gravettian culture was widespread throughout Europe, the Gravettians themselves clustered into two distinct genetic groups—one in the western Europe and one in central and eastern Europe. Now a new study [published](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128) in _Science Advances_ is blurring the lines between the two.

**Read more: “**[**Ice Age CSI: Mammoth Cold Case Files**](https://nautil.us/ice-age-csi-mammoth-cold-case-files-1281756)**”**

A team of paleogeneticists extracted DNA from several different Gravettian individuals who lived between 30,000 and 22,000 years ago in different parts of Europe and sequenced their genomes. One, a woman who lived in Isturitz Cave in southwestern France near the Spanish border, provided the oldest complete genome discovered in the region to date.

Combing through this treasure trove of genetic information, the researchers uncovered a fascinating clue about Gravettian life. According to the team, most sequences from the Isturitz woman’s genome matched those from other western European lineages, but she also carried genes from far off central and eastern Europe. Using genetic modeling, they were able to determine a pulse of gene flow from east to west likely occurred around 32,500–31,500 years ago.

“Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” study author Pere Gelabert of the University of Vienna explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148810). “Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected.”

The findings match genetic data recovered from another Gravettian individual who lived in Ormesson, France. According to the team, that could mean Isturitz was a hub of Gravettian activity, where a confluence of prehistoric peoples mingled and mated. If so, southern France’s reputation for romance extends back way farther than previously thought. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Multiple Births Can Accelerate A Mother’s Biological Age
content:
As any mom can tell you, having a baby takes a big toll. Growing an entire new human being inside your body demands a lot of resources, energy, and time and it can lead to dramatic physiological changes. There’s some evidence that child-bearing [benefits longevity](https://nautil.us/why-longevity-research-should-focus-on-women-1283406), but pregnancy can [accelerate biological aging](https://nautil.us/how-childbearing-leaves-its-imprint-on-mothers-biological-age-1261006) as well. Now, a new [review](http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.tem.2026.09.002) is trying to resolve this tension in the literature.

Two geneticists from Harvard Medical School surveyed data gathered from studies that measured the biological age of women using a variety of methods, including wearable devices, blood tests and epigenetic clocks, and brain imaging. They found that pregnancy seems to speed up the biological clock, but it slows back down postpartum.

**Read more: “[Pregnancy Changes Perception of Odors and Tastes](https://nautil.us/pregnancy-changes-perception-of-odors-and-tastes-237248)”**

The result of the review is a new framework for thinking about how timing pregnancies affects biological age. “Our previous research has found that biological age transiently rises during pregnancy, peaking around the third trimester or at the time of delivery,” study author Jesse Poganik of Harvard Medical School explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1147826). “If we accept the idea that these short-term changes in biological age occur, the question is how we can relate those changes to the overall trajectory of aging over the course of a lifetime.”

According to the team, spacing out pregnancies to allow time for the body to recover could be key to healthy aging. Interrupting that recovery interval with another pregnancy, on the other hand, could contribute to accelerated biological aging.

It’s a framework that’s in line with World Health Organization [guidelines](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/de7cfb95-b1c8-4286-aadf-5833fd3cab81/content), which recommend 24 months between pregnancies. However, the team stresses that more research should be conducted before developing any specific protocols for mothers. After all, the end product of the review is a hypothesis, and testing it will require closely following the health of women with multiple births over the course of their lives.

In the end, learning more about birth effects will contribute to a better understanding of aging in general. “There’s a lot of excitement about using biological age-assessment tools to guide individual health on a preventative and personalized level,” Poganik explained. “Studying changes during pregnancy is just one way to gain a more fundamental understanding of aging more broadly.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Was This the Exact Date of Van Gogh’s “Starry Night”?
content:
While _Starry Night_ is the traditional shorthand for Vincent van Gogh’s most famous work, its actual title is _The Starry Night_. It’s a more fitting name for such an iconic work, but does the painting depict an _actual_ starry night, or did it spring from van Gogh’s vivid imagination?

Art historians have debated the question for decades, but now astronomers are getting in on the action with a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-73025-5) in _Scientific Reports_. By taking a multidisciplinary approach that involves observational geometry, historical weather records, and even cicadas, they think they’ve nailed down the actual date of _The Starry Night_ in question.

**Read more: “[This Image from the Dark Energy Camera Is a Bit Van Gogh, No?](https://nautil.us/this-image-from-the-dark-energy-camera-is-a-bit-van-gogh-no-1283412)”**

Originally, van Gogh’s work was thought to be just an artistic representation of _a_ night sky. But when researchers surfaced a letter written by the painter mentioning Venus, some acknowledged that at least one of the painting’s swirly glowing orbs was inspired by a real celestial body. (You can see it just above the horizon, to the right of the cypress tree’s branch.)

In the 1980s, researchers started taking the painting seriously as an astronomical text. Using the position of the Venus orb as a lodestar and matching it to planetarium reconstructions of the night sky, art historian Albert Boime determined that three stars corresponded to the constellation Aries as it was visible from the location on June 19, 1889. The date came from letters van Gogh had sent to his brother, along with sketches of the work, detailing the painting.

There was one glaring problem with Boime’s analysis—the moon was all wrong. Looking out from the window of his asylum in late June, van Gogh would have seen a waning gibbous, not the slivered crescent he painted. This discrepancy, to Boime, was van Gogh taking a bit of artistic license. According to the historian, the glowing lunar penumbra and apparent paint scraped from the concave surface of the crescent indicate van Gogh may have painted the fuller gibbous, then changed his mind.

But per this new study, Biome’s analysis is incorrect, and the clue was the constellation he identified in the work. “To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in _The Starry Night_ is the Hyades in Taurus,” study author Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University in South Korea said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148245). “But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me.”

Kim and his colleagues proposed a new date for the painting. According to the team, van Gogh painted the pre-dawn sky of July 22, 1889. On that night, the Hyades (which form a V shape) would have been visible alongside Venus near the horizon and a crescent moon. In fact, the team’s shape analysis confirmed the correspondence between five central stars of _The Starry Night_ and the Hyades, and proved to be an even better match with a sketch van Gogh made after completing the painting.

So all the stars seemed to be aligned for a late July completion, but the team ran into another problem. Most scholars agree van Gogh suffered a seizure around mid-July that left him unable to paint for some time. If that timeline is correct, the researchers’ would be impossible.

To investigate, the team turned once again to van Gogh’s correspondences. In one letter, van Gogh said the seizure struck while painting on a windy day. Using weather records from the time, the researchers determined that there were only intermittent winds from the 15th to 26th of July, but strong mistral gusts starting on July 27th.

Additionally, van Gogh wrote about _The Starry Night_ along with other summer paintings, and specifically mentioned the sweltering climate and cicadas. While June only had four days above 86 degrees Fahrenheit (which the researchers say is cicada weather), July had eighteen, including over two weeks of consecutive scorchers.

Of course, none of this _proves_ that van Gogh painted _The Starry Night_ on the date in question, but it does suggest the day was the focal point of his observations, the researchers say. While we may never know for certain which starry night inspired the iconic painting, there’s one thing we can all agree on: It looks fantastic on a dorm room wall.

title: These Are the Most Stunning Weather Photos of the Year
content:
Weather conditions change second by second, which makes it a particularly dynamic subject for photographers. The violent and capricious nature of climate also makes for a fascinating theme for a photo contest. Enter: the American Meteorological Society (AMS), which highlights the best photos of “weather, water, and climate” around the world.

This year’s winners featured moon halos and rainbows, crashing waves, and banks of clouds. The shots came from all around the world too—from the shores of the Mediterranean to the plains of Texas.

You can see all the winners and finalists [here](https://headlines.ametsoc.org/photo-contest/). There’s a grand prize winner, together with second and third place entries, as well as a “member’s choice” selected by AMS members and an additional 26 shortlisted finalists. This year, submissions came from 1,075 photographers across 84 countries.

Some of our favorites are below…

The Grand Prize winner was “Diamond Dust Sky Eye” by Jaroslav Fous, taken in the Ore Mountains in Czechia using a Nikon D500 with a fish-eye lens. These halos are created as moonlight (or daylight) passes through crystals high up in Earth’s atmosphere. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

Second place went to “Sea Dragon,” captured by Chris Elkinton at Cape Disappointment on the Washington coast, using a Canon 90D. As the crashing waves bounced back from the rocky cliffs on the shoreline, this sea dragon shape appeared for the briefest of moments. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

Photographer Roberto Bueno titled this dramatic image “Cirrus, the Veils of the Moon.” The third-place winner was taken with an Olympus OM-1 along the Mediterranean in Spain. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

“Rainbow Cataclysm,” shot by Jeremy Janus with a Nikon Z6 in Denver, earned the Member’s Choice award. Janus says he was chasing the weather cell east for a couple of hours when this stunning rainbow emerged from the mammatus clouds. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

A range of incredible shots achieved finalist status. For example: “A Celestial Lightshow,” taken by Matthew Grahovac in the Dolly Sods wilderness area in West Virginia. It’s of the northern lights aurora shining above a grove of pine sentinels. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

“Lenticulars Above Mount Washington” by Ryan Steinke was snapped in New Hampshire. Lenticular clouds form as mountains push air rapidly upward, where it cools and condenses. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

Photographer Ibrahim Kandil captured “Diamond Dust” during a severe dust storm in Giza, near Cairo, Egypt. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

This snapshot of a storm above Lake Como in Italy was taken just as a lightning strike hit the ground. This image—appropriately named “Majestic Strike at Lake Como”—was the work of photographer Florian Ambrosino. _Credit: AMS Photo Contest 2026_

title: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
content:
[_This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked_]

In 1999, Professor Clark Elliott is rear-ended by a stranger at a stoplight. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine.

Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop.

In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday:

> “At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. I had lost the mysterious initiative that impels us all forward when we walk, and I knew that without brain rest I wouldn’t be getting it back. I considered lying down in the snow.”

Over an hour later, Elliott finally manages to cross the parking lot and begins the second phase of his trial: getting into the car.

“I’d lost the concept of center. I had no internal representation, or visual understanding of circle, target, middle, inside. Without these concepts I couldn’t get my hand to move toward the lock, or put the key in the slot.” So he just stands next to the door for another hour and a half.

Around 2 a.m., a suspicious police officer asks why Elliott is loitering in the parking lot, but the officer is too cold to get out of his car and drives away. At 3:30 a.m., four and a half hours after he left his office, Elliott finally arrives home.

Somehow, Elliott lives like this for a decade.

The book’s first mystery is how a person can remain conscious, verbal, employed, and yet so damaged that he can’t get into a car or recognize his own house. The second mystery is: why did he apparently recover through treatments that sound, at first pass, like boutique neuro-quackery?

A disclosure is in order before we continue. I am pretty personally invested in the answers here. About a year and a half ago, I got seriously concussed. Milder than Elliott’s, but bad enough to substantially rearrange my life. On some level, I read this book in hope of a cheap fix, or at least an obvious one. Instead I found myself in the weird borderlands of modern medicine.

What’s it like to be a human with severe brain damage? Elliott offers a metaphor:

_To simulate concussion damage to a human brain then, we’ll need to gather together […] 50 million desktop computers, a 500,000-mile-high stack of paper, and the almost inconceivable amount of information it takes to construct a human mind, then loose a hurricane on the system, ripping out network lines, laying waste to vast sections of memory, and sending landslides to smash hundreds of thousands of computers._

A bit sensational, but you get the picture. One classic model of what’s happening during severe concussions is “diffuse axonal injury”: rapid acceleration and deceleration stretch axons, the neuron projections that send electrical signals, causing micro-tears and disrupting cellular metabolism.

Standard CT and MRI imaging usually fail to detect these microscopic or functional disruptions, and there isn’t really a cure, so patients are told to go home, rest up, and wait to find out whether they’ll be back to work the next day or out of commission for the next decade.

U.S. concussion incidence is commonly cited around 1.6-3.8 million a year, and many go unreported[1](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-ghost-in-my#footnote-1) . About 15-30% of adults report post-concussion symptoms (PCS) 3-6 months later. Even on conservative estimates, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year in the US alone. A much smaller number of those cases will result in something like Elliott’s experience.

After the initial fender-bender, Elliott hands his driver’s license to the other driver. Then, a few minutes later, he hands it over again. He has no memory of having done so the first time, and can’t figure out why people are looking at him funny. This is a recurring theme—Elliott can’t even notice the problem, because the cognition that’s supposed to monitor the behavior has gone offline.

He writes: “when cognitive capabilities go missing they are often so fully gone that the concussive does not miss them in the way a normal person would, or indeed sometimes even realize they’ve gone absent.”

But Clark Elliott is no pushover. He’s a Professor of Artificial Intelligence at DePaul University, a consummate musician, is single-handedly renovating his family home, and runs marathons on the side. The biographical lists serve a purpose: Elliott wants to assure the reader that he hasn’t become _less intelligent._ His cognitive capacities have just come apart in a way that doesn’t track any nameable cognitive disorder.

He can write, but he cannot read. He can climb stairs but not descend them. He can teach a graduate seminar and then, walking home afterward, fail to recognize his own house. Moving through doorways or down halls poses a significant challenge.

More than once, he describes his state as “alien.” He writes, “we still walk and talk and act as though we are part of the human race, but it doesn’t feel that way inside… Instead, there is a strange feeling of nostalgia, a longing for who we used to be.” He notes that this feeling of disconnection is likely a significant contributor to the rate of suicide among concussives[2](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-ghost-in-my#footnote-2) : “we have, in many ways, already lost that which makes us human.”

One of the most striking passages in the book is when Elliott, hungry, decides to make himself a snack. He heads to the kitchen to eat a piece of salami and an apple, but finds he can’t. As though trapped in an old Tom and Jerry cartoon, he finds himself literally unable to choose which of the two to eat first. He can’t initiate action selection. He goes to the living room, returns to the kitchen, fails again. He repeats this loop ten times, like “a rat repeatedly traversing a dead-end maze.” _Two days pass before he eats_.

Elliott calls this “getting stuck.” The bridge between knowing what he wants to do and doing it has broken. In desperation, he finally calls his bemused friend Jake, who tells him: “Okay, go eat the salami first, then eat the apple,” ending the forty-eight hours of struggle.

Somehow, he cobbles together enough coping mechanisms to keep limping along for years. Until he can’t anymore.

“This is it,” Elliott reflected. “I am never going to have another normal day, or hour, or ten-minute period again. I am never going to be a real human being again. I won’t be publishing my research, and at some point I am going to lose my job.”

Ten years after the crash, Elliott is approaching a complete breakdown. Or rather, while broken, he adds a small child to the equation. As it turns out, the normal prattle of his two-year-old daughter is concussion kryptonite:

“It was this simple combination—my inability to filter out or process spoken dialogue in real time, and Erin’s continual need to talk—that almost led to a final, catastrophic meltdown.” He calls it “partial death.”

Unfortunately, there are no parenting sabbaticals. In a last-ditch effort, Elliott pulls out his emergency savings and reaches out to a “cognitive restructuring specialist” named Donalee Markus.

_Wait a minute_, you might be thinking. _Elliott hasn’t seen a specialist before??_

He has, sort of. It didn’t help. A brief detour through medical history: Elliott hit his head in 1999. The CDC didn’t publish its first major report on mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) until 2003. The NFL concussion crisis broke into public awareness in 2005. Until 2013, the only mention of persistent post-concussive symptoms in the DSM-IV was in the appendix under “proposed criteria set”. After the crash, an ER doctor checks his pupils and sends him home; a neurologist runs a 30-minute test and declares him fine, and shouts at him when he pushes back.

It’s unclear whether Elliott was just unlucky in encountering a cast of extremely unsympathetic medical professionals, or whether this was really the general state of neurology in the 90s. Whatever the case, Elliott quickly writes the whole system off and goes back to calling his friend Jake whenever he gets stuck in doorways.

For ten years, Elliott can’t make himself a sandwich. Then, over the course of a year, he substantially recovers. Enter idiosyncratic concussion specialists Donalee Markus and Deborah Zelinsky.

This is the first time we have a third-person perspective on Elliott. Markus writes:

“Clark Elliott was a mystery to me when we first met. Observing him through my glass front door, I saw that it took him two minutes just to find the doorknob with his hand. When I gave him the simplest of my assessment tests—copying a geometric line drawing—his body went into bizarre contortions as he struggled to complete it.” Markus takes him on as a patient anyway.

Her intervention is simple: she gives him geometric puzzles to solve, specifically trapezoids and three-dimensional dot exercises that escalate in complexity. He has to apply rules to shapes, generate equations from them, and eventually do the whole thing in his head.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XliJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff5c6f5b5-839f-4c0d-99ef-318148949dc5_941x634.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XliJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff5c6f5b5-839f-4c0d-99ef-318148949dc5_941x634.png)

[(Source)](https://www.amazon.com/Ghost-My-Brain-Concussion-Plasticity/dp/0143108298): Elliot includes a bunch of these geometric puzzle examples in the book. Sadly, they didn’t alleviate my symptoms.

Markus also refers Elliott to her colleague Deborah Zelinsky, a neuro-optometrist.

Zelinsky’s diagnostic method is a little more involved. The patient closes their eyes, and the examiner rings a small bell at various positions in space. The patient must reach out to touch the bell. The patient will often fail this test, revealing a “visual-auditory mismatch.” Zelinsky will then try different prism lens combinations _while the patient’s eyes are closed_ and ask them to do the bell test again. I repeat, the patient’s eyes remain fully closed. The entire time. She then prescribes the lenses that improve the patient’s performance.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wVWo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F621384df-793b-4ff7-bfc6-7b5c2ce23f2d_468x476.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wVWo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F621384df-793b-4ff7-bfc6-7b5c2ce23f2d_468x476.png)

[(Source).](https://mindeye.com/using-the-z-bell-test-to-remediate-spatial-deficiencies-in-non-image-forming-retinal-processing/) The only image I could find of the Z-bell test; fittingly grainy and hard to evaluate.

This is called the Z-bell test (presumably after “Zelinsky,” who has a patent on it). While I wasn’t particularly surprised that adjusting someone’s vision when their eyes are open can change how accurately they localize sound when their eyes are closed, I remain deeply confused about how prism lenses could alter accuracy if the patient’s eyes **remain closed the entire time.**

The claim is that low-level light still passes through the closed eyelids, stimulates retinal activity, and that this stimulation is what’s being modulated by the different lenses.

Zelinsky’s Mind-Eye Institute website:

> “By placing various types of lenses across a patient’s closed eyes, we can change the way light spreads over the retina, thus modifying the dynamic relationship between the mind’s visual inputs and the body’s internal responses.”

Depending on wavelength, eyelids transmit somewhere from well under 1% of blue/green light to around 5–6% of red light. But, as anyone with eyelids knows, this is still mostly diffuse reddish illumination—not sufficient to update your visual field, or to localize a bell.

But within a year of meeting Markus and Zelinsky, Elliott has experienced massive improvements and is on the road to recovery. He writes a heartfelt note to Markus thanking her for “giving him his life back.” So I guess the treatments worked?

Let’s take a look at the evidence, starting with Markus. Markus belongs to a fairly large tradition of “cognitive training interventions” for PCS for which there’s some evidence. A 2016 meta-analysis looking at 14 studies on cognitive training in post-acute TBI found a small effect on overall improvement in cognitive function (Hallock et al., 2016).

Unfortunately, “cognitive rehabilitation” is an enormous umbrella and Markus’s specific protocol isn’t in the meta-analysis. Markus published her own protocol in 2007, describing the puzzle-based technique she used on Elliott, but it’s more of a “how I do it” piece, not a controlled trial. The trail of scientific evidence dries up there.

Okay, what about Zelinsky? Do the bells work? There’s a 2019 paper that tried to find out. First author: Clark Elliott.

The paper is a preliminary conference paper on 14 out of the 41 recruited participants. Elliott et al. find that the therapeutic lenses produced a small but statistically significant improvement in bell-touching accuracy compared to the clear-lens baseline. However, the therapeutic lenses didn’t outperform an ‘impaired lens’ condition, which was theorized to push the outcome in the _opposite direction_, and the full study with all 41 recruited participants has never been published.

This is pretty tepid evidence. With one preliminary, ambiguous analysis its only empirical bulwark against the wave of scientific skepticism, Zelinsky’s method isn’t looking too good.

That said, the testimonial evidence is abundant. “I can move normally again, be active, travel. Mind-Eye has opened up a whole new chapter in my life,” says an avid patient. One testimonial describes the treatment as “like, well, ‘magic,’” while another patient calls it “mathemagical.”

We can add Clark Elliott to the rave reviewers. Within ten days of his first prism glasses, he reports a strange shift. Music sounds different, and he starts re-accessing visual scenes from childhood.

Within a month, Elliott begins to feel like himself again. The “ghost of his true self” had reentered the room. “At last I had enough brain power to support the real me, the complex me. I could see the world through my own eyes again.”

The strongest within-book evidence that the glasses, in particular, are doing causal work comes from what happens when Elliott briefly loses them. Even 33 hours without his prescription produces dramatic regression: exhaustion, handwriting deterioration, visual disturbances, and the return of the “all tasks involve pain in some way” baseline of his pre-recovery life. Once he finds the glasses, he’s back to playing the Beatles from memory and “looking forward to the rest of [his life] again.”

Elliott is writing the book fifteen years after the accident, and the recovery has held. He even claims, with the partial qualification one expects from a man who has nearly lost his mind to a brain injury, that his cognition is in some ways now better than it was before the crash.

A skeptical explanation might be that Elliott was desperate and ripe for placebo effect. Receiving intense attention from clinicians who believed they could help him after years of failed encounters with doctors might have been sufficient to shift his symptoms. Elliott’s recovery was staged over five years with iterative adjustments, which is exactly the protocol that would maintain a placebo effect, and the base rate of spontaneous recovery in chronic PCS is non-zero. So can we be sure that any of these treatments did anything other than give him a pat on the back as the concussion worked itself out?

I think a case can be made for at least some real intervention. While the evidence for Zelinsky’s closed-eye method in particular is thin, the general “prescribe new lenses” approach looks much more promising. There’s even a reasonable causal mechanism on offer.

If you hold up your thumb in front of your face, and then easily switch between looking at something on the wall and your thumb, congrats - your accommodation triad is working. The accommodation triad is the trio of ocular functions that enable close-up vision. In many PCS patients, this system goes awry, resulting in a suite of vision complications. In a study of adolescent patients (n=116), Wiecek et al (2021) found that ~60% of patients had deficits in near point of convergence after concussion. Prism lenses can reduce eye strain by shifting the image on the retina so the eyes don’t have to work as hard to converge, and magnifying lenses reduce accommodation demand.

A year into my concussion, and partially inspired by Elliott, I asked my neuro-opthalmologist for prism lenses. They didn’t help at all. But the magnifying lenses I tried next _totally did_, almost entirely eliminating my symptoms immediately (unfortunately, they later returned).

It’s possible that Zelinsky’s method actually does work, but not for the reason she thinks. The bell ceremony might just be an unusually elaborate way to arrive at a genuinely useful prescription.

This would explain both her rave reviews and the lack of scientific support. Her Z-bell tinkering isn’t doing much, but the broader lens intervention sometimes works—some percent of the time, prism glasses and magnifying lenses actually _do_ improve people’s concussion symptoms. (Of course, this will result in a hit-or-miss treatment, but you can’t tell because none of the duds post a review).

So what, if anything, can we learn from Elliott’s recovery?

Here’s one obvious point: recovery is possible, but strangely elusive. It took Elliott a decade, several awful medical encounters, and two boutique specialists to find help. While the situation was worse in the 90s, it’s still bad today. In one study, among patients severe enough to reach specialty care, fewer than a third had recovered when surveyed, and the still-symptomatic group had been living with PCS for an average of 4.5 years (Hiploylee et al., 2017).

Perhaps the real mystery is: why is it so hard to treat concussions?

One reason is that concussions resist mainstream medical intervention. Clinical instruments can’t catch the microscopic damage common to PCS, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) struggle to identify treatments when the population is heterogeneous and the symptoms are varied and subjective. So it takes months to get a PCS diagnosis, and even when you do, many clinicians have no idea what to do with you.

PCS treatment is hard because concussion does not damage an abstract, average brain. It damages _your_ brain, with your particular foibles and weak spots. Specialist concussion medicine has identified roughly six clinical phenotypes, but even when correctly type-cast, each patient responds differently. Clark Elliott and I both had vision issues, but he responded to prisms while magnifying lenses worked for me. PCS may be less like a single disease than a family resemblance category with wildly different failures compressed into one diagnosis.

RCTs are the “medical gold standard.” But perhaps idiosyncratic medical maladies are where the standard hierarchy of evidence breaks down a little. Philosopher of science Nancy Cartwright has argued that RCTs answer a narrower question than clinical practice needs: they tell you that a treatment, on average, produced a particular outcome in a trial population. They don’t tell you whether it will work for _you in particular._

So PCS patients navigate the uncanny valley of niche medical science: on the one side, RCTs and rigorous studies that document average effects that might not apply to you, and on the other, N=1 case studies that might solve your exact problem, or be entirely useless. In the middle, there’s a bunch of people trying to sell you metabolism-enhancing lasers for five thousand dollars. Absent clear explanations, patients can find themselves passed between neurologists, optometrists, physical therapists, vision therapists, acupuncturists, psychiatrists, and energy-healers before finding the one thing that happens to work for them.

To get the most juice out of a clinical trial, you need a theory of why the treatment worked, for whom, and whether you’re similar enough to the trial population for the effect to transfer.

But what if you don’t have a mature theory yet?

As a species, we’ve been solving problems we don’t understand for a long time. On Fiji’s Yasawa Island, pregnant and breastfeeding women observe taboos against eating certain species of reef fish. When Natalie and Joseph Henrich investigated in 2010, they found that the taboo species mapped onto the fish most likely to carry ciguatera toxin, a naturally occurring marine toxin that’s particularly dangerous to fetuses and nursing infants. Local variation combined with fitness-relevant outcomes and social learning can surface solutions long before the mechanism is understood. (The trade-off is that sometimes they suggest you try bloodletting or child sacrifice).

For poorly understood chronic conditions, treatment often looks less like applying established science and more like janky cultural learning. PCS communities generate variation, share outcomes online, and copy apparently successful interventions.

But what makes the Fijian case work is that there’s a real selector pulling signal out of the noise. Toxic fish made people visibly sick, and useful taboos could be reinforced across generations. The PCS testimonial ecosystem has no comparably reliable selector; variants can propagate just because they’re dramatic or recent or someone’s trying to sell you something. The same dynamics that make it kind of reasonable to try Zelinsky’s Z-bell test might push you toward forty sessions of hyperbaric oxygen at $200 a pop.

Another drawback is that cultural transmission is good at producing outcomes, but overimitates methods. The Z-bell case is actually a nice illustration. Even if Zelinsky’s lenses actually help some patients, the community’s causal story (closed-eye retinal stimulation) might be totally wrong. Cultural transmission will faithfully convey the bells-and-mathemagic ritual along with whatever genuinely works.

Alright, clearly we can’t just trust the forums. In an ideal world, we’d capitalize on the strengths of patient communities (lots of people trying lots of things) and combine it with some kind of rigorous selection mechanism.

Luckily, there’s already a proof of concept for this. In 2020, the Body Politic COVID support group pioneered a novel idea: ask patients stuff. They created the Patient-Generated Hypotheses Journal (PGHJ) and began advising (and funding) major research efforts. Their flagship peer-reviewed paper (Davis et al, 2021), an online survey of 3,762 people drawn from support groups across 56 countries, found that Long COVID affected multiple organ systems, that symptoms persisted well past acute infection, and that recovery often took many months (all borne out by subsequent research).

Some community-amplified hypotheses won’t hold up—great, that’s what science is for! At the least, the PGHJ demonstrates that heterogenous patient communities can do more than swap miracle stories; they can generate structured observations and funnel hypotheses toward controlled studies. For example, do prism glasses actually improve general cognitive functioning in PCS patients with convergence issues? Despite Elliott’s popularization, as far as I can tell there are _literally no RCTs testing this._

For medical orphans like PCS, the evidence hierarchy is doing the right things in the wrong order. Population-wide RCTs belong at the top once we know what outcome we care about and what mechanism we’re targeting. Until then, structured patient case registries could help us figure out what actually deserves a trial.

Two years ago, if someone asked me how to navigate PCS, I would have said, “Uh, only pursue treatments with clear, scientifically-backed benefits.”

And at first, that’s what I did. My path to recovery started with best-evidenced treatments. But as the months dragged on without improvement, I found myself in testimonial-land—trying things based on Google Maps reviews, and reading this book.

As a concussion roadmap, _The Ghost in My Brain_ is pretty frustrating. Elliott is too ready to accept his clinicians’ explanations and treats his recovery path as way more generalizable than it is. But as phenomenology, it’s excellent. It does a great job of conveying what it _feels like_ when your brain breaks. If you’re intrigued by the extreme edges of human experience, this is for you. If you’re looking for a guidebook, sorry, there isn’t one (yet).

For conditions like severe, persistent PCS, the patients who recover often fall into two groups: the ones who are lucky enough to find clinicians willing to iterate with them, and the ones who have the time and money to experiment on themselves. That’s a small slice of the population.

We can’t just replace RCTs with facebook groups, but maybe we could bridge the weirdness of individual cases and the discipline of controlled science. The rather dark irony here is that the PCS patient community has PCS. Many of us can’t look at screens, nevermind organize case registries. But if even the conservative end of the PCS estimates is right, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year. Many of those people are doing exactly what I did—trawling through forums and trying treatments. And whether or not anyone records the results, people will continue to search the solution space. Because when your brain breaks and you’re stuck in apple vs salami hell, you try all the bells and prisms.

[1](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-ghost-in-my#footnote-anchor-1)

Institute of Medicine and National Research Council. _Sports-Related Concussions in Youth: Improving the Science, Changing the Culture_. National Academies Press, 2014, citing Langlois et al. 2006. This is technically a report on sports and recreation-related TBI and concussion, which are overlapping categories that both often lead to PCS. Given that this is _just_ sports and rec related, the real number must be much higher.

[2](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-ghost-in-my#footnote-anchor-2)

A major JAMA Neurology meta-analysis found a relative risk of suicide of 2.03 after concussion/mild TBI. In two included cohort studies with about 4 years median follow-up, suicide deaths occurred in 0.50% and 0.59% of diagnosed concussion/mTBI patients. That is roughly 1 in 200 over that follow-up period

title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
content:
To invade red blood cells, the deadly protists create temporary molecular portals that disappear behind them — doors we can now see in fine detail.

![Image 1: An illustration shows a small parasite, in stages, pressing into a central red blood cell. Surrounding blood vessels show the blood cell infection in its different stages.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MalariaPortal-cr-Ada-Zejun-Shen-Lede-scaled.webp)

_Plasmodium_, the parasite that causes malaria, invades and proliferates inside red blood cells. Researchers imaged the proteins (dark purple ovals) it places on the cell membrane that let it slip through unnoticed.

Ada Zejun Shen for _Quanta Magazine_

## Introduction

In medieval Italy, it was accepted wisdom that anyone walking near a swamp risked falling ill from “bad air” — _mala aria_. Victims were struck with fever, headache, nausea, and chills, and occasionally the illness escalated to vomiting, jaundice, and death. Today, we still call this affliction malaria. For much of human history, it has ravaged populations in humid tropical and subtropical regions, killing untold numbers. In the 20th century, it was responsible for [up to 5% of deaths (opens a new tab)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK215638/) worldwide; it still kills [approximately 600,000 people (opens a new tab)](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria) each year.

What malaria was and how it infected humans was deeply mysterious until barely 150 years ago. In 1880, the French physician [Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran (opens a new tab)](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1907/laveran/facts/) peered at a sample of a soldier’s blood through a crude microscope and discovered the true cause of the disease: not miasma, but a genus of shape-shifting single-celled protists called _Plasmodium_. Since then, scientists and doctors have described in precise detail the parasites’ life cycle, hosts, and disease progression, and even the nuances of various _Plasmodium_ species, which present slightly different forms of the disease. But some crucial aspects have remained a mystery.

For example, _Plasmodium_ invades human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. To get in, the microbe creates a ring-shaped structure called the moving junction, which briefly creates a gap in the cell membrane it can slip through. The gap then disappears without a trace. It opens and closes so rapidly, at such a small scale, that imaging technologies couldn’t capture it. Researchers had no clue what the portal structure actually looked like. “Because of that,” said [Chi-Min Ho (opens a new tab)](https://microbiology.columbia.edu/faculty-chi-min-ho), a microbiologist and structural biologist at Columbia University, “we didn’t really know anything about how it works.”

Now, Ho’s lab has [imaged the moving junction (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.06.012) right at the moment of invasion, in unprecedented detail. Her team found that when the _Plasmodium_ parasite installs molecular gaskets in the host cell, it radically remodels the cell membrane to slip through without a trace. This knowledge could help inform the next generation of malaria treatments and influence the drug-discovery process for other parasitic diseases, such as cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis.

“It’s a totally mind-blowing paper,” said [Jake Baum (opens a new tab)](https://www.unsw.edu.au/staff/jake-baum), a parasitologist at the University of New South Wales, who was not involved in the research. “At the end of the day, this is not molecular biology. This is biophysics.”

## **Home Remodeling**

The history of malaria research has paralleled advances in microscopy, from the development of simple light microscopes like the one Laveran used to the cutting-edge cryo-electron techniques of Ho’s lab. This is because the cells the microbes invade are extremely tiny — and the parasites are even smaller. At about 8 micrometers across, red blood cells are among the smallest cells in the human body, and all species of _Plasmodium_ are a fraction of that size during the invasion stage.

Attempts to image the parasites in the act of breaking and entering got off the ground in the 1970s, when pioneering microbiologists first applied electron microscopy. These scientists observed a distinct thickening of the cellular membrane near the parasite’s access point. Then the tiny, round _Plasmodium_ seemed to simply merge with the cell, like a water droplet coalescing into a larger pool. It would be decades before techniques developed enough to isolate the proteins that make this possible, much less image them.

Another hurdle is that malaria parasites have [a very complicated life cycle (opens a new tab)](https://www.cdc.gov/dpdx/malaria/index.html). They are most at home in the gut of a mosquito where they can reproduce sexually. Humans are what’s known as a reservoir host — a place for the parasite to live while it waits to be taken up by an insect.

“The food supply happens to be our red blood cells,” said [Kirk Deitsch (opens a new tab)](https://amrcenter.cornell.edu/people/kirk-deitsch/), a microbiologist and immunologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York. “That’s why they’re invading us.”

To this end, the _Plasmodium_ parasite assumes [a variety of shapes and sizes (opens a new tab)](https://www.cdc.gov/dpdx/resources/pdf/benchaids/malaria/malaria_comparison_p3-6.pdf) as it moves through its life stages: Sometimes it’s shaped like an egg, sometimes a spindly thread, sometimes a gangly starfish. It can move through this cycle in rapid succession or hang out in one stage (the hypnozoite phase in the human liver) for years. When it enters its tiny, round merozoite stage, the parasite is ready to invade a red blood cell.

_Plasmodium_ pulls up to the scene of the crime with all the proteins and other biological equipment it needs. The entry procedure is more delicate than simply punching a hole in the host cell. “If you’re trying to push an orange into a balloon, the balloon mustn’t pop, right?” Baum said.

Based on previous research, scientists knew the broad strokes of this process. The parasite approaches a host red blood cell and inserts a ring of protein anchors into the cell’s membrane. Collectively these anchors are known as the moving junction. _Plasmodium_ locks into them with proteins expressed on its surface — and then pushes forward. The moving junction forms a continuous portal in the host cell membrane for the parasite to travel through. Once the parasite is fully inside, the cell membrane seals up behind it. The whole process takes less than a minute.

Ho and the other authors of the new paper used cryo-electron microscopy to probe the four individual protein units in each anchor. What they learned allowed them to propose a more detailed model for how the moving junction actively remodels the host cell’s membrane. The parasite injects into the red blood cell three proteins, which form a dense wedge beneath the membrane surface; a fourth protein connects this structure to the invader. _Plasmodium_ places many of these anchors on the red blood cell surface. The proteins produce electrostatic forces and pressure in the cell membrane, which crowd and displace its lipid molecules. This deforms the membrane and reverses its curvature. It bows slightly inward around the parasite — in fact, some lipids slough off and reassemble into a protective membrane for the invader — before re-forming and sealing behind it.

“It’s a really nice example of how a field has built step by step by step toward a really powerful observation,” Baum said.

Once inside, _Plasmodium_ approaches its remodeling work more comprehensively. Red blood cells are essentially bags of hemoglobin; they have no nucleus or organelles to speak of. So _Plasmodium_ builds from the ground up. It secretes proteins that allow it to feed on hemoglobin, remove waste, and stretch the cell’s cytoplasm. Ho compared it to the conversion of an empty warehouse floor into a stylish lofted apartment.

“It’s putting in plumbing,” she said. “It’s putting in the floors. It’s literally building everything for itself.”

In this process, the parasite also redecorates the cell’s exterior. It is equipped with genes that allow it to make a series of distinct but closely related adhesive proteins that it can express on the red blood cell’s surface. These proteins cause the cells to stick to the walls of the blood vessels around them — one of the main causes of malaria’s painful symptoms. In 2025, [research from Deitsch’s lab (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-025-02008-5) found that by periodically switching between proteins, the parasite can avoid tipping off the immune system to its presence for days or weeks at a time. Such extensive exterior cellular remodeling serves a purpose: It helps _Plasmodium_ avoid a trip to the spleen, an organ that filters out dead, defective, or broken red blood cells as well as any undercover parasites.

![Image 2: Electron micrograph shows a group of bialy-like red blood cells. The central cell is covered in many small bumps, evidence of its malaria infection.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Red_blood_with_malaria-Rick-Fairhurst-and-Jordan-Zuspann-National-Institute-of-Allergy-and-Infectious-Diseases-National-Institutes-of-Health.webp)

Protrusions called knobs cover the surface of an infected red blood cell. _Plasmodium_, the parasite that causes malaria, expresses these proteins after it invades the cell. They make cells clump to the walls of blood vessels, causing the disease’s most dangerous symptoms including organ distress, seizures, and coma.

Rick Fairhurst and Jordan Zuspann, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health

The parasite itself undergoes a radical change inside the cell. It transforms from a roundish merozoite into an amoebalike trophozoite. It grows several cytoplasm “arms” and flattens out, said [Christiaan van Ooij (opens a new tab)](https://www.keele.ac.uk/lifesci/ourpeople/christiaanvanooij/), a molecular parasitologist at Keele University in the United Kingdom. This also helps it evade the immune system. The trophozoite shape is more flexible than that of the spherical merozoite, and the immune system clocks supple cells as healthy and stiff cells as dead.

The parasite then replicates asexually for about 48 hours, dividing inside the red blood cell until it’s so full of _Plasmodium_ that it bursts. Like house flippers, the parasites move on to other blood cells. Within days, millions could be lurking in the bloodstream.

In this way, malaria can quickly overwhelm a human host. It is all enabled by the moving junction that allows the parasites to set up shop without tipping off the authorities. The structure of the moving junction could help researchers intervene, with drugs to block the parasite from invading a host blood cell in the first place.

## **Moving Target**

Malaria treatment has long been something of a hit-or-miss proposition. Without a granular view of how _Plasmodium_ interacts with host cells, researchers had to test various compounds by trial and error. If a given drug seemed to fight the illness, they had little idea what part of the infection process it had disrupted. “All that work was done essentially blind,” Deitsch said.

This has made developing new malaria treatments notoriously difficult. The former workhorse antimalarial drugs, such as chloroquine, sulfadoxine, and pyrimethamine, are now known to target the parasites in the bloodstream. But the _Plasmodium_ species that infect humans are [rapidly evolving resistance to these compounds (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpddr.2025.100602).

Invasion offers a tantalizing choke point for new medicines. “If you block invasion, then you stop the parasite in its tracks,” Ho said. To make her point, her team used [an AI-powered protein-design platform (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09429-6) to craft an inhibitory protein that could block the moving junction. In test tubes, it prevented _Plasmodium_ from entering red blood cells. But its safety and efficacy haven’t been tested in animal models.

It’s possible that the moving junction could be something of a skeleton key that could be used to treat other parasitic diseases. _Plasmodium_ is a member of the apicomplexans, a large phylum of parasitic protists that also includes _Toxoplasma gondii_, a cat parasite, and _Cyclospora_, which causes explosive diarrhea. These single-celled organisms appear to enter using the same biochemical equipment as _Plasmodium_. “All of these are parasites that have this invasion machinery,” Deitsch said. The study of those conditions could in turn inform malaria treatment. A 2026 paper [described the mechanism (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-026-00911-z) by which _Toxoplasma_ senses the right moment to deploy its moving junction, and malaria may operate the same way.

But the moving junction may prove to be too much of a moving target. “Some people have always argued that invasion is a really bad drug target because it’s a very short process,” van Ooij said. Any drug with the ability to stop invasion would have a roughly 60-second window in which to do so, which means it would need to remain stable in the body for a long time or act extremely quickly, or both.

Ho’s team already has their sights set on another target. They plan to use similar cryo-electron microscopy techniques to solve the structure of other protein complexes involved in malaria infection, such as those adhesive proteins that keep infected blood cells from journeying to the spleen.

“We’ve caught one white whale,” Ho said. “So we want to go after the other remaining white whales.”

title: How to Be Transformed When Things Fall Apart
content:
[![Image 1: How to Be Transformed When Things Fall Apart](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/whenthingsfallapart_chodron.jpg?fit=320%2C506&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/When-Things-Fall-Apart-Anniversary/dp/1611803438/?tag=braipick-20)

In every life, there comes a time when we are razed to the bone of our resilience by losses beyond our control — lacerations of the heart that feel barely bearable, that leave us bereft of solid ground. What then?

_“In art,”_ Kafka [assured](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/07/03/kafka-music-art/) his teenage walking companion, _“one must throw one’s life away in order to gain it.”_ As in art, so in life — so suggests the American Tibetan Buddhist nun and teacher **Pema Chödrön**. In [**_When Things Fall Apart: Heart Advice for Difficult Times_**](https://www.amazon.com/When-Things-Fall-Apart-Anniversary/dp/1611803438/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/when-things-fall-apart-heart-advice-for-difficult-times/oclc/923548256&referer=brief_results)), she draws on her own confrontation with personal crisis and on the ancient teachings of Tibetan Buddhism to offer gentle and incisive guidance to the enormity we stand to gain during those times when all seems to be lost. Half a century after Albert Camus asserted that [“there is no love of life without despair of life,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/30/albert-camus-travel-lyrical-critical-essays/) Chödrön reframes those moments of acute despair as opportunities for befriending life by befriending ourselves in the deepest sense.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/fog.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/liminal-worlds-by-maria-popova_print?curator=brainpicker)

“Liminal Worlds” by Maria Popova. Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/liminal-worlds-by-maria-popova_print?curator=brainpicker).

Writing in that Buddhist way of wrapping in simple language the difficult and beautiful truths of existence, Chödrön examines the most elemental human response to the uncharted territory that comes with loss or any other species of unforeseen change:

> Fear is a universal experience. Even the smallest insect feels it. We wade in the tidal pools and put our finger near the soft, open bodies of sea anemones and they close up. Everything spontaneously does that. It’s not a terrible thing that we feel fear when faced with the unknown. It is part of being alive, something we all share. We react against the possibility of loneliness, of death, of not having anything to hold on to. Fear is a natural reaction to moving closer to the truth.
> 
> 
> If we commit ourselves to staying right where we are, then our experience becomes very vivid. Things become very clear when there is nowhere to escape.

This clarity, Chödrön argues, is a matter of becoming intimate with fear and rather than treating it as a problem to be solved, using it as a tool with which to dismantle all of our familiar structures of being, “a complete undoing of old ways of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and thinking.” Noting that bravery is not the absence of fear but the intimacy with fear, she writes:

> When we really begin to do this, we’re going to be continually humbled. There’s not going to be much room for the arrogance that holding on to ideals can bring. The arrogance that inevitably does arise is going to be continually shot down by our own courage to step forward a little further. The kinds of discoveries that are made through practice have nothing to do with believing in anything. They have much more to do with having the courage to die, the courage to die continually.

In essence, this is the hard work of befriending ourselves, which is our only mechanism for befriending life in its completeness. Out of that, Chödrön argues, arises our deepest strength:

> Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Things falling apart is a kind of testing and also a kind of healing. We think that the point is to pass the test or to overcome the problem, but the truth is that things don’t really get solved. They come together and they fall apart. Then they come together again and fall apart again. It’s just like that. The healing comes from letting there be room for all of this to happen: room for grief, for relief, for misery, for joy.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/tree_by_MariaPopova.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/brokenhearted-by-maria-popova_print?curator=brainpicker)

“Broken/hearted” by Maria Popova. Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/brokenhearted-by-maria-popova_print?curator=brainpicker).

Decades after Rollo May made his case for [the constructiveness of despair](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/30/freedom-and-destiny-rollo-may-despair-joy/), Chödrön considers the fundamental choice we have in facing our unsettlement — whether with aggressive aversion or with generative openness to possibility:

> Life is a good teacher and a good friend. Things are always in transition, if we could only realize it. Nothing ever sums itself up in the way that we like to dream about. The off-center, in-between state is an ideal situation, a situation in which we don’t get caught and we can open our hearts and minds beyond limit. It’s a very tender, nonaggressive, open-ended state of affairs.
> 
> 
> To stay with that shakiness — to stay with a broken heart, with a rumbling stomach, with the feeling of hopelessness and wanting to get revenge — that is the path of true awakening. Sticking with that uncertainty, getting the knack of relaxing in the midst of chaos, learning not to panic — this is the spiritual path. Getting the knack of catching ourselves, of gently and compassionately catching ourselves, is the path of the warrior. We catch ourselves one zillion times as once again, whether we like it or not, we harden into resentment, bitterness, righteous indignation — harden in any way, even into a sense of relief, a sense of inspiration.

Half a century after Alan Watts began introducing Eastern teachings into the West with his [clarion call for presence as the antidote to anxiety](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/01/06/alan-watts-wisdom-of-insecurity-1/), Chödrön points to the present moment — however uncertain, however difficult — as the sole seedbed of wakefulness to all of life:

> This very moment is the perfect teacher, and it’s always with us.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> We can be with what’s happening and not dissociate. Awakeness is found in our pleasure and our pain, our confusion and our wisdom, available in each moment of our weird, unfathomable, ordinary everyday lives.

[![Image 4](https://i1.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/lisberthzwerger_grimm19.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/07/20/best-brothers-grimm-illustrations/)

Illustration by Lisbeth Zwerger from a [special edition of the Brothers Grimm fairy tales](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/07/20/best-brothers-grimm-illustrations/)

Remaining present and intimate with the moment, she argues, requires mastering _maitri_ — the Buddhist practice of loving-kindness toward oneself, that [most difficult art of self-compassion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/09/05/school-of-life-self-compassion/). She contrasts _maitri_ with the typical Western therapy and self-help method of handling crises:

> What makes _maitri_ such a different approach is that we are not trying to solve a problem. We are not striving to make pain go away or to become a better person. In fact, we are giving up control altogether and letting concepts and ideals fall apart. This starts with realizing that whatever occurs is neither the beginning nor the end. It is just the same kind of normal human experience that’s been happening to everyday people from the beginning of time. Thoughts, emotions, moods, and memories come and they go, and basic nowness is always here.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> In the midst of all the heavy dialogue with ourselves, open space is always there.

Another Buddhist concept at odds with our Western coping mechanisms is the Tibetan expression _ye tang che_. Chödrön explains its connotations, evocative of Camus’s insistence on the vitalizing power of despair:

> The _ye_ part means “totally, completely,” and the rest of it means “exhausted.” Altogether, _ye tang che means_ totally tired out. We might say “totally fed up.” It describes an experience of complete hopelessness, of completely giving up hope. This is an important point. This is the beginning of the beginning. Without giving up hope — that there’s somewhere better to be, that there’s someone better to be — we will never relax with where we are or who we are.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Suffering begins to dissolve when we can question the belief or the hope that there’s anywhere to hide.

Decades after Simone de Beauvoir’s proclamation about [atheism and the ultimate frontier of hope](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/01/25/simone-de-beauvoir-optimism-pessimism-hoipe/), Chödrön points out that at the heart of Buddhism’s approach is not the escapism of religion but the realism of secular philosophy. And yet these crude demarcations fail to capture the subtlety of these teachings. She clarifies:

> The difference between theism and nontheism is not whether one does or does not believe in God… Theism is a deep-seated conviction that there’s some hand to hold: if we just do the right things, someone will appreciate us and take care of us. It means thinking there’s always going to be a babysitter available when we need one. We all are inclined to abdicate our responsibilities and delegate our authority to something outside ourselves. Nontheism is relaxing with the ambiguity and uncertainty of the present moment without reaching for anything to protect ourselves.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Hopelessness is the basic ground. Otherwise, we’re going to make the journey with the hope of getting security… Begin the journey without hope of getting ground under your feet. Begin with hopelessness.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> When inspiration has become hidden, when we feel ready to give up, this is the time when healing can be found in the tenderness of pain itself… In the midst of loneliness, in the midst of fear, in the middle of feeling misunderstood and rejected is the heartbeat of all things.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/lionandbird_dubuc17.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/07/the-lion-and-the-bird-marianne-dubuc/)

Art from [_The Lion and the Bird_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/07/the-lion-and-the-bird-marianne-dubuc/) by Marianne Dubuc

Only through such active self-compassion to our own darkness, Chödrön suggests, can we begin to offer authentic light to anybody else, to become a force of radiance in the world. She writes:

> We don’t set out to save the world; we set out to wonder how other people are doing and to reflect on how our actions affect other people’s hearts.

Complement the immensely grounding and elevating [**_When Things Fall Apart_**](https://www.amazon.com/When-Things-Fall-Apart-Anniversary/dp/1611803438/?tag=braipick-20) with Camus on [strength of character in times of trouble](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/12/28/albert-camus-almond-trees-character/), Erich Fromm on [what self-love really means](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/04/27/erich-fromm-sane-society-self-love/), and Nietzsche on [why a fulfilling life requires embracing rather than running from difficulty](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/15/nietzsche-on-difficulty/), then revisit Chödrön on [the art of letting go](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/01/19/pema-chodron-the-wisdom-of-no-escape/).

# The Wildest Bet Is the Winning Bet

### By Maria Popova

We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable. It helps to remember that we ourselves are children of improbability, that everything we treasure exists not because it had to, not because it was likely or necessary, but because the universe took a gamble against the staggering odds otherwise.
